# R5 — Justification

Every semantic unit of `artifact/library/core/rules/R5-code-before-docs.md`, why
it exists, what breaks if it is removed, and where the idea comes from. Source
numbers refer to `SOURCES.md`.

| # | Unit | Why it exists | What breaks if removed | Source / inspiration |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Title and rule paragraph ("Write the smallest code…; a doc is a map, not the territory") | Fixes the order in one line — code and its test first, prose second — and names what a doc may contain at all: a projection with pointers, not a copy of the behavior. "Smallest" stops a framework before a mechanic. | The rule degrades to "document your code", which every project already believes and none follows; or it is obeyed with a short but complete restatement of the code, which is the same duplication one page long. | 5 (Django: docs document features added since the last release), 6 (Clippy: documentation is the last step before the PR), 4 (raylib: the whole surface on one page, detail in examples) |
| 2 | Why paragraph ("a guess with a deadline attached… cannot fail") | Names the mechanism, not the value: prose has no exit code, so drift is invisible. Without a mechanism the rule reads as style advice and is the first line cut. | The rule is deleted the first time a deadline is tight, because "we should document less" sounds like laziness rather than a defect fix. | 2 (a proposal is not an implementation), project history (v0.2: 87k words, contradictions, no build) |
| 3 | Order step 1: one sentence of intent | Allows the minimum needed to start work without opening the door to a full spec; one sentence cannot hide a design. | The agent either writes nothing down (and re-invents the mechanic) or writes a GDD to be safe. | 7 (MDN separates "what we write" from "how we write") |
| 4 | Order step 2: smallest working code + one test that fails before and passes after (R1) | Puts the proof inside the order, so "tested" is a step rather than an afterthought; points at R1 instead of restating its evidence table. | Code arrives without a test and the doc inherits unverified claims; or the test arrives after the doc and validates the prose. | 6 (Clippy: test then lint, both before merge), 5 (Django: regression test as the default attachment) |
| 5 | Order step 3: run it, play it, stop if not approved | Splits "works" from "approved". A mechanic can pass its test and still be wrong for the game; documenting it then is documenting a discard. | Docs are written for mechanics that a playtest kills, and the project pays to maintain decisions it has reversed. | 3 (Godot demo projects: the artifact is played, not read) |
| 6 | Order step 4: then the doc, one page (D06) | Binds the rule to an existing template instead of inventing a document type; D06 carries the fields. | The doc becomes free-form, grows, and duplicates the code it describes. | 1 (Godot: class reference derived from the engine source), 6 (Clippy: doc comment written last) |
| 7 | "A doc written at step 1 is a plan. A plan is not a mechanic." | Closes the argument that a short design sketch is harmless; it is harmless only if everyone knows it is not the deliverable. | Each pre-code doc is defended as "just a sketch", and the sketch set becomes the 87k words. | 2 (ideas for unbuilt features live in a separate proposals repo) |
| 8 | Behavior bullet (code wins until the doc is corrected; never edit the test to match prose) | Settles every future disagreement in one direction, and blocks the cheap resolution of "fixing" the check. | Two directions coexist; the weaker one (edit the test) wins because it is faster and makes everything green. | 1 (docs derived from source, not maintained in parallel) |
| 9 | Intent bullet (why, feel, decision, how to work on it) | Defines what a doc is *for*, so the rule cannot be read as "write no docs". It also names the content code cannot carry. | The rule is obeyed by writing nothing, and the next developer has behavior with no rationale. | 7 (MDN: guidelines say what we write, not just how), 8 (a dedicated place for context) |
| 10 | Cite-the-proof bullet (`verified by:`, test or `evidence/` path, S02) | Makes each doc sentence falsifiable; a claim without a check is the only kind that can rot silently. | Docs become assertions again; a reader cannot tell a current fact from a 2024 guess. | 5 (Django runs docs checks in CI before merge), 1 (R1/S02 evidence paths) |
| 11 | One page, one fact bullet (link, never restate) | Two copies of a fact drift, and the reader trusts whichever they opened first. The link is also what keeps a small doc set navigable. | The same number appears in three files; a tuning change must find all three, which E01 then fails. | 8 (AGENTS.md: one dedicated, predictable place), 9 (hierarchical context with discovery boundaries) |
| 12 | Delta-not-rewrite bullet | A rewrite makes the diff unreviewable, so nobody checks it, and an error introduced during "polish" survives. | Every small change regenerates a document; review cost rises and history stops explaining the current text. | 5 (Django `versionchanged` notes collect a release's changes instead of rewriting the section) |
| 13 | Not allowed: GDD or design document for an unbuilt system | The specific artifact that caused the failure, named so it cannot be reintroduced under a new name. | The rule is satisfied by renaming the GDD to "design note" or "system overview". | 2 (proposals live in their own repo; the manual documents the engine as it is) |
| 14 | Not allowed: roadmap, "we will implement this later", future tense | Future tense in a system doc is an unmarked promise; a reader cannot separate it from current behavior. Roadmaps also duplicate BACKLOG (R9). | Docs become half-spec, half-status, and no sentence can be trusted without checking the build. | 9 (R9 scope is budget: ideas live in one backlog), 5 (Django documents only what was added) |
| 15 | Not allowed: intended behavior written as if current | The most expensive single error: it reads as evidence of a mechanic that does not exist. | A reviewer accepts a feature on the strength of a sentence; the build has no such feature. | 1 (reference text must match the shipped engine), 5 (docs describe added features only) |
| 16 | Allowed: `BRIEF.md` (D01) before the first prototype | Without a named legal exception the first prototype is blocked, and the agent writes the GDD after all to be safe. | Either the rule is broken on day one (and loses authority) or prototyping stalls on paperwork. | Blueprint D01; 3 (a demo starts from a stated question) |
| 17 | Allowed: `DECISIONS.md` (D03) after a real choice | A decision has no test and no code, so it needs its own one-line record; "after a real choice" keeps it from becoming a diary. | Decisions are re-litigated weekly, or the doc set grows a narrative "design log" that restates the system cards. | Blueprint D03; 8 (a predictable place for context) |
| 18 | Allowed: system card (D06) after the mechanic works and was played | Names the moment the doc becomes legal, matching step 3; "was played" uses R8/G1 as the approval test without redefining it. | Cards are written on approval-by-assertion and describe intent that no one has felt. | 6 (doc written after the code compiles and tests pass), R8 |
| 19 | Docs lint: three checks (page limit, links, `verified by`) | A check nobody runs is decoration; three cheap checks catch the three real failures (growth, dead links, uncited claims) without a docs toolchain. | Docs grow past one page and links rot silently; or a full linter is built and maintained instead of the game. | 5 (Django `make check` in CI, docs checks must pass before merge), 4 (raylib keeps the reference to one page) |
| 20 | Check line (E01, R1, R6, "delete the claim") | Gives the rule a cheap existing test (E01 counts touched docs) and states the boundary with R1 and R6 so three parts do not restate one idea. "Delete the claim" is the smallest repair when no proof exists. | The rule has no observable failure, and its edges with R1/R6 blur until two documents disagree about which one applies. | Blueprint E01; 9 (one fact in one place), rubric §1 duplication |

## Deliberate omissions

| Omitted | Reason |
|---|---|
| The fields of a system card | D06 owns them; repeating them here creates the second copy this rule forbids. |
| A definition of "approved" or "played" | R8 and G1 own the fun test; R5 only requires that some human played it before the card is written. |
| A page-size number (words, lines, characters) | D06 says "one page"; a second number in a rule drifts from the template. The lint check reads the limit from the template. |
| The docs-lint implementation | CLI07 `doctor` already checks links and encoding; R5 states the three checks, not the tool. |
| Per-doc language rules (EN / RU) | The blueprint's Documents section and D01–D09 own language; a rule-level copy would contradict D10. |
| A worked example of a good doc | D06 is the example; an inline sample doubles the size and rots first. |
| A "documentation" skill | S02 `verify` already cites evidence; a second skill would be an addition without a repeated failure, which R6 forbids. |
| Changelog and release notes | X03 owns changelog; release notes are a delta mechanism but sit outside the daily doc set. |
| Diagram, ADR, or comment conventions | Not part of the failure this rule addresses; adding them would make R5 a style guide. |
